## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

A single-fascicle verse treatise attributed to [陳那菩薩](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E9%82%A3%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9) **Dignāga** (c. 480–540), translated by [真諦](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%9C%9F%E8%AB%A6) **Paramārtha** in the Liáng-Chén period (between 557 and 569). Preserved in the *Taishō* at T31n1620. The work is the **earlier of two extant Chinese translations** of the same Sanskrit work; the second is [KR6n0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6n/KR6n0119) *Zhǎngzhōng lùn* 掌中論 (T31n1621), translated by [義淨](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%BE%A9%E6%B7%A8) **Yìjìng**. The Sanskrit *Hastavāla-prakaraṇa* (also titled *Hastābhavaprakaraṇa*) is preserved as a Tibetan and partly as a Sanskrit witness; modern scholarship has reattributed it to **Āryadeva** rather than Dignāga, but the Chinese tradition uniformly preserves the Dignāga attribution. The catalog meta retains the traditional Dignāga ascription.

**Abstract**

The *Jiějuǎn lùn* / *Hastavāla-prakaraṇa* is a short verse-and-prose treatise demonstrating that conventional objects (*saṃvṛti-sat*) — like the snake-on-the-rope, like the cloth on the loom — are mere designations imposed by mind on what are at base only nominal aggregations. The title metaphor — "releasing the fist" (*hastavāla* in the closed-fist / open-palm sense, here glossed as "the fist that releases its grip on objects") — is the frame for a doctrine close to the *prajñāpāramitā* analysis of the conventional. The work is thus a Yogācāra-flavoured restatement of the *Madhyamaka* analysis of conventional truth, fitting the contested attribution between Dignāga and Āryadeva.

[真諦](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%9C%9F%E8%AB%A6) Paramārtha's translation, like the parallel [KR6n0111](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6n/KR6n0111) *Wúxiāng sīchén lùn*, dates from his productive late Chén period at *Zhìzhǐsì* in Guǎngzhōu (557–569). It is one of his more compact translation projects and forms part of the early Chinese reception of the Dignāga (or Āryadeva) corpus that fed into the late-sixth-century Shèlùn 攝論-school synthesis.
